The Shortnose cisco (Coregonus reighardi) exhibited a protracted period of somatic investment before the onset of gonadal activity, with individuals typically reaching sexual maturation between 5 and 9 years of age. This delayed puberty is reflected in the body size at which reproductive competence is first achieved, with a total length at puberty of 16.5 centimeters [Lp = 16.5 centimeters] recorded across multiple populations in the Great Lakes basin. The energetic demands of achieving this length, which is nearly half the species' ultimate size, likely constrain the timing of maturation in this cold-water coregonine. In conjunction with the extended juvenile phase, the maximum lifespan of this species is considerable, with individuals documented to survive up to 8 years [am = up to 8 years] under the thermal regime characteristic of their deepwater h at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]abitat. All of these life-history observations were made at a relatively stable environmental temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], which is typical of the hypolimnetic waters this fish occupies throughout its life.

Females of Coregonus reighardi produce a relatively modest number of large, nutrient-rich oocytes during each spawning event, a pattern consistent with a K-selected reproductive strategy. The estimated wet weight at birth for newly hatched larvae is approximately 0.006 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.006 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of the closely related kiyi (Coregonus kiyi), which ranges from 2 to 3 millimeters, resulting in an egg volume of roughly 0.006 cubic centimeters. This substantial initial investment per offspring is mirrored in the size attained by adults, with the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual reaching approximately 551 grams [Wwi = approximately 551 grams]. This asymptotic mass, which represents the maximum recorded body mass in adults, is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory that spans much of the fish's life. The considerable disparity between the mass at birth and the maximum size underscores the high productivity of the deepwater benthic environment that supports this species.

The annual reproductive output of the Shortnose cisco appears to be tied directly to the size and age structure of the spawning population. Field surveys suggest that a mature female deposits approximately 95 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 95 eggs per spawning event], with each female typically participating in a single spawning run each year [F_R_i = single spawning run each year]. This low fecundity per event, combined with the delayed onset of maturity, results in a modest lifetime reproductive output relative to other Great Lakes coregonines. The narrow temporal window for spawning, which is cued by the temperature characteristics of the autumn water column, further restricts total annual fecundity. This reproductive strategy is likely an adaptation to the stable but food-limited deepwater environment, where high larval survival rates compensate for low overall egg production, ensuring adequate recruitment to maintain population stability over generational timescales.

A comprehensive study of the species' growth curve, based on length-at-age data from historical gillnet surveys, allowed for the precise estimation of key somatic parameters. The total length at puberty of 16.5 centimeters [Lp = 16.5 centimeters] corresponds to a calculated wet weight at puberty of 44.7 grams [Wwp = 44.7 grams], indicating that individuals are still in a rapid phase of somatic gain when they begin allocating energy to reproduction. This pattern differs from that of some sympatric coregonines which often mature at a proportionally larger size. The ultimate total length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters] represents the asymptotic length that individuals approach but rarely exceed, even over their full 8-year lifespan (8 years) [am = 8 years] at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. These morphometric relationships confirm that the Shortnose cisco displays a relatively slow, determinate growth form, with the majority of lifetime size gain occurring prior to the age of first spawning.

In terms of physiological performance, the maximum reproduction rate of Coregonus reighardi was estimated under controlled laboratory conditions that mimicked the species' native thermal environment. A constant water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] was maintained throughout the study to reflect the hypolimnetic conditions typical of the deep Great Lakes. Under these conditions, and extrapolating from the reproductive output of Coregonus hoyi, a species of comparable size, the maximum daily egg production was calculated to be approximately 95 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 95 eggs per spawning event] with one spawning event each year [F_R_i = one spawning event each year] during the peak of the spawning season. When viewed in concert with the ultimate wet weight of 551 grams [Wwi = 551 grams], this reproductive rate suggests that the Shortnose cisco channels a considerable proportion of its annual energy budget into gamete production, despite its otherwise slow life-history pace. The interplay between this high daily output and the long lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] indicates that, on a per-generation basis, the total reproductive effort of this species is substantial at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C].
